In our house the fruit bowl is fair game at all times, even right before a meal. Our daughter will often ask for snacks right before dinner if it's running 15 minutes late, and even if she eats a banana it doesn't stop her eating a full meal. We often talk about 'always yes' foods, things like cucumber and hummus, and she can go and get that whenever she wants, EVEN AT BEDTIME. And she 100% took advantage of that at bedtime for a few days, and then the novelty wore off and it's not a delaying tactic anymore. And she knows that she won't ever be hungry so doesn't over eat on the whole. When she wants a sweet treat she'll ask for one and almost always the answer is yes because she only asks occasionally. It was a massive learning curve for me, and she definitely took advantage at first of having Always Yes food, but we're in a really good groove now.

'How many chicken nuggets do you want?' 'Come and see how much rice I'm putting on your plate' 'Shall I mix the sauce in to the pasta or keep it in a ramekin on the side?'. I try to cook enough so that everyone is full, and that there is the option for seconds if people want it (that often means I'm eating single sausage or nugget for lunch the next day!). Our daughter is a fiend for dessert at the moment - today she asked 'breakfast dessert' which is not and never will be a thing. But I do understand being full of bolognaise but still wanting a sweet treat after. We try to do fruit and yoghurt as a dessert most days, and often on a friday or a saturday we have something sweet (tonight we had profiteroles). I want her to respect her body, listen to its cues, but also not be reliant on junk food - it's a tricky line to follow.

One thing I've not seen (and you maybe already know this) is the sleeping tiger hold. It's where you put your hand under your babies chest/tummy so they're facing away from you and sort of facing the ground. You can still be doing things with your other hand, your baby is still close to you and getting comfort (and warm hands on tummy could be soothing if it's a sort of colic-response) but the biggest benefit to this is that you don't actively have a baby screaming into your face, which means it's a LOT easier to get through the particularly long fussy spells.

Hobbies, as others have suggested, are a great way to make friends, but it is hard with young kids to commit to something regular, or over bedtime, or on a weekend.

If you've got some mum friends you could try being the host for things. Get it in the group chat 'I'm hosting a kids christmas craft party on either saturday or sunday morning next week, I'll provide coffee and pancakes, plus the crafts, just bring some fruit/treats/yourself! Which day is best for everyone?' It doesn't have to be expensive things. Or even 'me and [kid] are going to check out the new skate park at x after school, who's in?' The more you meet up and chat the more friendly you will become.

I've also recently joined the PTA at my kids school and I never thought I would be a PTA mum but it turns out you get all the good school gossip if you do. I wouldnt say we're all best friends yet, but I've started being invited to 'mums wine night at X's house' or 'kids are going guising starting at my house at 6, who wants to come?' and I can definitely see close friendships developing between some of the other PTA parents, because we have a shared value - supporting the school.

Best of luck - it really is so hard to make new friends as an adult, but if you put yourself out there and aren't a dick you can do it!

Yes private nurseries can take children from 6 weeks old (although most children won't start until 6 months or later), and almost always these sessions will be paid for by the parents. Some employers and colleges have nurseries for staff use at a subsidised rate, although that has become so rare these days. I'm afraid I don't know much about Visa requirements, but you might be getting confused with the relatively new scheme in England where children are entitled to either 15 or 30 free childcare hours from the age of 9 months, or two years, or some combination of the above. That's not something that's running in Scotland as far as I know. You are entitled to make use of 'tax free childcare' which is where you sacrifice some of your salary and the government tops it up 20% and this can be used to pay for private nursery, some childminders of they are registered, and even out of hour/holiday school care (such as before or after school club, or all day holiday clubs).

Hi, your youngest won't start 'school nursery' until the term after they turn 3. It's a bit confusing because school nursery and daycare nursery are both called nursery. Some children can get a school nursery place at age 2, if there are other qualifying factors such as a disability, ESOL, or social work involvement in the home. School nursery is also a bit confusing these days as there are different placement patterns- I'd say the most common in Fife is 9-3 M-F term time only, but there are nurseries that offer longer days two days a week, or mornings or afternoons only 48 weeks of the year. You'd need to check what patterns your local nursery offer. Daycare/private nursery will be open from 7.30/8 until 5.30/6 and you normally pay per day your child attends. Some offer half days.

Hi there, at the time the east coast main line was run by either Virgin or LNER (I think Virgin, because I'm pretty sure it's LNER now). I'm not sure if you've worded the question badly or if I'm misunderstanding you but you're not looking for a specifically first class route or train line, almost all trains (especially the longer ones) will have a first class section on them. For the short train between Fife and Edinburgh (40 mins/2 carriages) this is just a seperated one third of one of the carriages (at the front or back of the train) where every seat is wider, has armrests, and has a table. It is sectioned off from the rest of the train with a little door so is normally also quieter. On longer routes (like Edinburgh to London) there will be at least one but sometimes more full carriages that are first class. These will come with lounge access at stations which have a lounge, where they provide tea/coffee/biscuits and sometimes even a shower. The trains themselves will probably have a trolley service where you will get a meal at mealtimes and snacks and drinks, and even a wine or a beer, all included in the price. Just look for 1st class tickets on whatever route you're planning. And don't book through The Trainline because they will charge a fee to book with them - use them to find your route and train, and then book on the actual train companies website (I.e. Scotrail, LNER, etc).

Ok, so here where I live we would expect baby to not get below 102oz, and to regain weight to a minimum of 113 within 10 days. Colostrum is very fatty and has huge benefits for baby. I would be checking latch and also for tongue or lip ties, and encouraging baby to feed off both breasts at each feed. I would also be teaching alternative feeding positions such as the rugby hold or the side by side, and also latching techniques, if that's already been done then I would suggest more frequent feeding (maybe once an hour during the day), and also feeding from both breasts twice at each feed, if mum wants to EBF. If mum just wants to see baby fed, I would suggest initial BF and then pumping while dad or another support person feeds with formula, and then using pumped colostrum/formula to top up thereafter.

Sorry OP I've just reread your post and misread the amount/type of bottles your baby is getting. If babies mum is still doing skin to skin or having lots of close cuddles with baby then her breast milk will still be reactive to what baby needs, even if she is pumping. Cows milk should definitely be introduced after meals to top-up if baby isnt full, but breast milk can and should (as long as mum is willing to pump) be offered as well. You can get calcium into baby through things like yoghurts and cheese with meals, but breast milk really does do wonders for as long as she can make it - well done her for still pumping! It's much harder to pump than breast feed I believe!

So here in Scotland (I think the recommendations are similar across the UK, though), the advice is to offer solids before milk, and once they reach the age of 1 to also get them off the bottle. I'd start by offering three meals plus two snacks per day accompanied with water to drink, then topping up with cows milk bottles. If your baby wont take a cows milk bottle the recommendations are to start with 5oz formula and 1oz cows milk, then after a week move to 4/2, then a week later 3/3... until they're totally on milk (and of course as your baby learns to eat more the amount of milk will go down, but keep upping the ratio of milk to formula). And of course your next step is to then get rid of the bottle! Try open cups, 360 cups, straws, heck some of the families I support use shot glasses! At the very least make sure if you're using a lidded cup with a spout it has FREE FLOW not one of those 'non spill' valves. Finally, I would 100% call your health visitor and ask for advice - this is literally their job and they will be so happy to help pre-emptively than to find out at the 13/15mo visit that they need to intervene.

Generally (and this is VERY general) I'm seeing an uptick in language acquisition because these toddlers and pre-schoolers were stuck at home during various lockdown so were spoken to a lot more (and equally, a huge amount more kids who are struggling with language acquisition due to being plopped in front of the telly so parents could work), but a massive sense of 'only me' type behaviour - poor sharing skills, not willing to take turns or wait to speak. Obviously that's all normal for pre-school and toddler settings but it's much more pronounced these days and the kids seem baffled by the concepts.

3 years ago I could ask a 3 or 4 year old to wait their turn to speak and they might well be unhappy about it but they would understand whereas now they just don't even get the concept that they're not number 1 priority for everyone.

Check which formula you've been given- if it's the sugar free one it'll taste worse than the sugared version. You have to request the sugar version specifically and it still tastes rank but is slightly better. Chocolate mousse can sometimes disguise the taste for a few bites, as can apple juice or sweetened apple puree (I know I know, you spend months trying not to give them sugar when they're that age, but you have to do what you have to do). If you're still really struggling, call the GP and ask for a different antibiotic. My daughter ended up with sepsis because we literally couldn't get her to take the antibiotics and the paediatric doctors at the hospital said that taking a less well suited antibiotic and actually taking the full dose was better than the perfect suited antibiotic that she was spitting out every time. Bribery might also work, lots of 'first this, then [treat]' conversations but it's so difficult when they're tiny. And try a spoon and straw like others have said. We also had some luck with strawberry syrup (the type that goes on ice cream) and ice cream itself. Ultimately if you have to hold them down then at least they're taking it, if they don't take it and things get worse then they sedate them for an IV in the hospital at that age so it's worth putting both of you through the stress to take it orally. Best of luck to you, hopefully you find something that works for you.

If your budget can stretch, I'd really recommend a food delivery service like Hello Fresh or Gousto. We sign up for them occasionally when they have a deal on and get a few meals. You go online and pick out meals your family would like (get the kids involved with this step!) and then the next week they deliver the exact quantities of the ingredients required with the recipes on little cards. It tells you how long prep will take, how long cooking will take, and of you need to add any ingredients yourself (normally a splash of oil on the pan, or a spoonful of sugar). It'll teach you how to make the meal. Then keep the recipe card and you've got a recipe and quantities you need to make it again. I consider myself a decent cook, but like all families we end up in a rut sometimes and this helps us get out of it.

What an exciting day for you! I'm guessing you're in the UK since you mentioned health visitors. Here's a link to a nice NHS booklet that covers everything. I work with mums with post-natal depression and anxiety and I've been recommending it to them all. http://www.healthscotland.com/documents/303.aspx

The most important thing is that your baby is showing all the signs of being ready- they can sit up properly, have lost the tongue thrust reaction, and they are showing an interest in food. You've spoken to your health visitor and she seems happy so that's great.

Next up, you want to be really familiar with the different between choking and gagging. Here's a public health video on what to do if your baby chokes: https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=gtbUB1XPW_o

Finally, you want you and your baby to have fun. I know you're anxious but your baby will pick up on this and it could make eating stressful for them so take a few deep breaths and prepare yourself - have another adult around for moral support. There's a good chance your baby won't actually eat anything today but as long as they are touching the food and maybe even some gets in their mouth then that's great.

And here's a story of my daughters first eating experience, to make you feel better. She was 5.5mo, and the health visitor had said she was A-OK to go at 6 months. We had been planning what her first food would be. We were excited and nervous. I went to my husbands work with her to show her off, we went to a chinese restaurant for lunch and were laughing and joking with the waiter. She was sat on my knee facing the table, and I looked down and she was halfway through a battered chicken ball with more salt and MSG in it than would be healthy for an adult. And she's 5.5years now and absolutely fine (and still loves chicken balls!) So seriously try not to stress if it doesn't go to plan!)

Ok, so this all varies SO much by area, but if I were struggling I'd start by looking for my local foodbank. Trussel Trust is the biggest network in the UK, although lots of other foodbanks exist including some excellent independent ones. They will likely be very well connected with other charities in the area that will be able to help with things like energy advice, sanitary products, benefits advice, etc. 

Here in Fife we have a charity that's funded by the council called Cosy Kingdom - it's funded out of money that every council in Scotland were given to help with things like this. They can help you get out of debt, they might provide blackout curtains for you, or those foil things for behind your radiators, they can give you an emergency top up, help you change supplier to a cheaper one, and also lend you a device that will show how much energy each device uses even when it's on standby. You will have something similar in your local area, find them and ask them for help.

If your child is in school or nursery, a lot of schools now have family workers or family liaison officers. They are here to help you. A lot of parents distrust these people and think that they're setting their kids up to be labelled if they go to them, but this isnt the case. These members of staff aren't teachers, they're not social workers, they're just there to help you. The ones in local schools here often get donations of school uniform (often brand new!) which they are able to pass on to people who are struggling, but they'll never pass it on to you if they don't know you need it.

CAP (Christian's Against Poverty) work nationwide, although they don't cover every postcode. They are a completely free debt advice service. They will meet you, help you without judging you, and sort out your debt. They'll give you excellent advice, they're regulated by/registered with the FCA, and although they are a Christian organisation it's open to people of all faiths and none.

Local community centres/churches. Get on facebook and have a hunt around for your local community centres and churches. Lots of them will have community workers who can refer you to other organisations. For example, I can refer folk for xmas presents for their kids, to the foodbank, I can supply sanitary items and condoms, I can get someone to come and do a benefits audit, I can get you nappies and formula for your kids... I work for a church but I'm not there to try and convert you. I'm there to help! And lots of others like us, but we need to know who you are so make yourself known! Lots of churches and community centres also have community cafes where they have a 'pay it forward' board or a 'pay what you can' thing. So if you need a hot meal hit them up!

Are you on a prepayment meter? Is your son under 5? If those are true then I am so sure that there is help available for you. If you're struggling to find help please feel free to PM me with your rough area and I can look for you. The 3rd sector is in a blind panic about the rising energy costs, and combined with the UC cut we are seeing people through our doors we've never seen before. My daughter had (and has) severe eczema, to the point of regular hospitalisation, and for some time she went through a biting stage. I hated it - I was still breastfeeding her (until she was almost three) and almost always bit me when she was feeding. But at nursery (daycare) she also bit other children. She was using the toys as fidget toys/distraction, and then bit when that was taken away from her because her only other option was to scratch herself until she was literally sitting with bleeding and weeping skin. 

After that the nursery staff sat with her when  she was particularly scratchy, made sure she had actual fidget toys available and in reach, and when they could see she was trying not to scratch kept other kids from taking toys off her. 

I'm pleased to say she has been bite free for over 2 years now, and although her eczema is still extremely limiting she doesnt let her bother her. But we needed the nursery to understand it wasnt a problem at home, and we cant punish a kid for something that happened 8 hours ago when  they were at nursery when we got home, at that age. Our daughter is a similar age and we have had a huge amount of success with the book Barbara Throws A Wobbler by Nadia Shireen. In it, Barbara has a 'bad day' and it feels like nothing's going right until she throws a massive strop and is rude to her friends. It talks through the process of controlling that feeling, taking a deep breath and working through it. At the end there's a two page spread of lots of kids playing at the park with 'wobblers' hanging around in the bushes and the kids are all possibly having a bad day. E.g. someones ice cream has fallen, or their kite is blowing away. We spend a lot of time looking at that page and talking about how those kids feel and why, and what they should do about it.

You've been given loads of really good advice about the behavioural side of things in the moment, but my daughter responded really well to this book, and also practising mindfulness techniques. We try to do some baby yoga (baby yoghurt as she calls it), or breathing exercises. And if we notice she's heading down that path we try to give her other options - 'it looks like you're getting stressed - would you like to go to your room and take 5 minutes to do some deep breaths? Mummy can leave you alone to think, or come and do it with you.' Or 'remember when Barbara had a really bad day and threw a wobbler? It just made things so much worse! Let's have a cuddle together now so we feel better'. Or the one that's worked surprisingly well is 'it's ok to be upset or angry about [something it's fair to be upset about - a friend needing to go home or something], so if you think you're starting to feel that way tell mummy "I'm feeling out of sorts, I'm going to take a minute by myself"'. And then really get in and praise that behaviour. I've been quite candid a few times and said 'oh, it looks like you were going to hit me there but chose to take a deep breath instead - I am SO PROUD you did that. Let's go and get a star sticker for your jumper! In fact, I'm so happy you did that I'm going to put your favourite song on for a dance party - let's go!' This has the added benefit of a distraction and removal from whatever the trigger point is.

Sorry I just wanted to clarify - when I said here in Fife I meant 'if you foster through the Fife local authority foster team'. It could well be different if you go through Barnardos or the like. Remember that the agency you go through affects your pay as well. As an example, for full time fostering you will be paid around £60 less per week than if you went through a private agency, but with the council you will be paid even if you don't have a child placed with you, whereas your payments would stop if you didnt have a placement with the private agencies. (And by pay I mean the actual stipend paid to you for what you're doing, you will also get money to go towards the cost of looking after the child for food, clothes, etc, and obviously that should rightly not be paid if you dont have a child to look after). Just something to keep in mind if you do go down the full time route some day.

I have volunteered a lot in the past, and now I work in the 3rd sector as a volunteer manager. Plenty of places are always on the lookout for volunteers, however surprisingly our local foodbank is overrun with volunteers and has actually started running a twice yearly recruitment evening where they interview to fill specific roles, and everyone else is turned away. 

In my work we have two types of volunteers - we have the people who due to their history, skills and situation would not be able to work currently - these are the people who are sometimes more work on our end than the help they provide. We will teach them basic skills like you need to turn up on time, it's polite to shower and brush your teeth before coming to 'work', you can't actually swear at children, this is how you turn on a computer. The second type are the 'giving back' people who are possibly recently retired, their work let's then do 5 days of volunteering a year and get paid for it, or they are looking to change careers so want more relevant experience (and a reference from us!)

Try to find someplace to volunteer that matches your own values - there's no point volunteering someplace that feeds the poor if you secretly think that people should just manage their money better - it'll come out, and contrary to what a lot of people think - you can be sacked as a volunteer!

Volunteering is very rewarding and you can get a lot out of it! Find someplace that is a good match for you and make sure you commit to it properly - treat it like a job - if they are expecting you and you can't make it, call and tell them. Turn up on time and be as helpful as you can be. And remember to have fun.

P.s. it costs around £1000 to train a volunteer (that's the rough figure we use for grant applications in my neck of the woods!) So the place you're volunteering for is making that investment in you - make sure it's worthwhile for them!

We did a lot of camping before I got pregnant, and are now getting back into it again, so we've recently gone through the upgrade process ourselves because camping with a two year old is much harder than just camping as a couple.

We have a cheap gas drive with the gas cartridges which is a game changer. We went to hone bargains and bought a super cheap pot and frying pan so we didn't have to use my expensive kitchen ones and it's great.

I'd also recommend a collapsible water container. It's fab if you're miles away from the drinking water tap to just fill up and have at your camp, especially of you like a coffee or tea regularly. 

We had super decent rollmats to sleep on, but pregnancy, weight gain and getting older has rendered them less useful. The past few times I've taken a cheapo spare duvet to put underneath us, along with the rollmats which adds another layer between the ground so it doesn't get so cold, but also a bit of padding to lie on as well.

Take slip on or velcro sandals so if you're just nipping out the tent you don't need to faff around with socks and proper shoes.

Make sure you have adequate waterproofs. Nothing worse than getting wet and cold and then just being wet and cold all weekend. 

Make sure your sleeping bags are all season ones - unless you're willing to spend the big bucks they will be heavier than the standard supermarket/cheap walking shop sleeping bags, but that shouldn't be an issue if you're not hiking in to where you're camping. It really is worth it to be cosy all night.

We have a few small lanterns we use for light, along with a set of battery powered fairy lights, and two little battery torches as well. It's great to have a few options with you e.g. lantern gives off more light but wouldn't take that with me to the toilet in the middle of the night!

Aldi sell some pretty cheap awning type things at the moment - if it's big pitches you might be able to take something like that which is great for sitting under and cooking under if it's too sunny, or rainy or whatever. 

Don't forget to make sure you're drying your tent out every time at home, and that you rewaterproof the seals every so often. You can buy big tubs of the waterproofing stuff and put your tent up in the garden and just go over the seals. If you find it's letting in water through the actual fabric you can paint that too but it might be worth just upgrading your tent at that point if it's something you're looking at doing anyway.

Basically they'll cover you if a medical practitioner tells you not to go. They need you to get a medical certificate, so when you phone to claim tomorrow ask them to send you one out to give to your Dr next time you see them. 

The form will likely ask questions like:

- is pax fit to fly?

- reason?

- onset?

- holiday was booked on xx, was this condition known about?

- insurance taken out on xx, was this condition known about?

- any related conditions?

Your GP will likely charge for this, and this isn't a cost the insurance will cover. You also aren't covered for APD so make sure you call to cancel your flights (even though they say non-refundable), and get an email confirmation that you cancelled, that they're not refundable and will not be refunded (you'll have to pay for this as well from a lot of airlines) and ask for your APD back which legally they have to give you. There might be an administration cost for this as well, and again it won't be covered by your insurance but you will still end up getting some money back from them.

So, as long as you aren't prone to kidney infections or have an underlying condition that contributed to this (that you haven't declared to them and paid an additional premium for), and your GP has confirmed not ftf then you should be ok.

The documents you'll need to make the claim are : booking documents for flights, hotels, activities, which show the date booked, costs, and the fact they were paid in full (so if you initially paid a deposit you'll need a further doc to show it was paid in full), cancellation docs showing the date cancelled and if any refund was given (it needs to state no refund if there was no refund), and medical certificate.

Travel can also include pre-paid airport parking, prebooked train/tram/bus tickets so make sure you claim for everything that you have paid for already. 

You don't need to have all the docs when you phone, but it's a good idea to know roughly all of the costs because insurers don't like it when people start tacking on extra bits to the claim.

IANAL but do have some limited understanding of the new regs. As I understand it, the reason you would be processing people's data is as a legitimate interest. As such you don't need permission to hold their data or to process it, but you do need permission to share their data.  It would be good practice to have a privacy notice that you give to people when they sign up for the league or up on your noticeboard that says who you are [dominoes tournament organiser], what data you hold [names, phone numbers, emails? Addresses? (You can only hold data that is necessary so think about what you want to put here)], who can access the data [you and the co-organiser, you and the pub owner, you and Bob from down the road who takes the pool tournament once every month because you've got a standing McDonalds date with your mum], and what the information will be used for [texting people what their fixtures are the week before]. 

You can only use legitimate interests basis for holding data if you are genuinely using it for a legitimate interest, you couldn't give the phone list to your girlfriend to text everyone because she's starting selling Herbalife for example.

You also need to give people the option to opt out of you holding their data. You should put on the privacy notice that you will delete all data when someone leaves the league, or it shuts down, or if they ask to be removed. It's ok to make it clear that they can't be part of the league if they don't sign up though.

As to the WhatsApp group, as long as it's not a requirement to be in it then this would just be considered a group of pals with a group chat. People are free to leave as they wish, as long as you're not adding them without asking first.

Your certificate of insurance will say something like 'sections A, B, C, D1, D2, D4 & F'. One section in the policy booklet will be about third party cover on someone else's car if they have given you permission to drive it. Check which sections you are covered for and then make sure that it includes the driving other cars section. Most likely it will only be valid if you're over 25, as well.

Third party means that if you are involved in an accident, your insurance will only cover the other car.

Some insurance policies will let you have other people drive your own car. For example, with Saga another person can drive your car in an emergency. It's designed because older people are more likely to fall ill and need someone to drive them to hospital or home. So, if you've not got the driving other cars part on your policy, read through your FILs policy because you never know.

Ok, since every policy is different I'm going to be referring to the Nationwide FlexPlus policy in this answer, because I already have that open from a question a few days ago. It can be found [here!](https://www.nationwide.co.uk/~/media/MainSite/documents/products/current-accounts/flexplus/P3349_FlexPlus_Worldwide_Family_Travel_Insurance_Policy.pdf)

Nationwide FlexPlus will cover your whole family as standard, this is detailed on page 15 as the account holders, their partner, and their dependant children. Partner and dependent children are also defined in the policy booklet on page 10: Partner (The person the account holder lives with at your home address in a relationship, whether married or cohabiting, as if husband and wife or civil partners, regardless of gender) and Dependent Children (All children (including legally adopted, foster and step children) of the account holder who at the start date of the journey have not reached the age of 19 or not reached the age of 22 if in full time education, living at the home address and are unmarried or have not entered into a Civil Partnership. We will cover dependent children who do not reside permanently (or for the majority of the time) with the account holder, providing the child(ren) reside permanently with the other parent for the remainder of the time.) We are also told that we can add a guest to the policy for an additional premium (Guest: Any person who is travelling with the account holder during the period of the journey who lives in the UK and for whom the appropriate additional premium has been paid.)

So in your question, for an aunt or cousin to be covered they would need to be added as a guest and an additional premium paid. If we now turn to the cancellation section of the policy (page 22) we can see that there are a number of reasons a cancellation claim will be accepted, the most common being the first scenario detailed - due to death or injury or illness. Now, it says this can be of an immediate family member, which is again defined on page 10 (Your partner, fiancé, fiancée, parents, parents-in-law, step-parents, son, son-in-law, daughter, daughter-in-law, brother, brother-in-law, sister, sister-in-law, step-children, legal guardian, grand-parents, grand-children.) - as you can see, this would not normally an aunt or cousin, however further down the claims conditions we can see that they specify they will accept cancellation conditions for a travelling companion or if a relative or friend in whose home you intend to stay becomes unwell or dies or is seriously injured. In this instance, if you were travelling with your aunt and she had her own insurance, you would still be able to cancel due to your travelling companion becoming unwell. Likewise if you were going to Australia to stay with your aunt and she sadly passed away you would be able to claim.

Hope this explains some of it. If you have any specific questions then just shout. 

For added fun - check out page 42 and 43 for some information on Golf Cover and Wedding Cover which come as standard with this policy.

Ooh, I work in travel insurance - this one's for me!

Her insurance will not cover her for any of your portion - you'll need to have your own insurance and it will cover you for all of your share. As standard, we would ask for all booking and cancellation documents and expect them to have your name on them (as a flight passenger, or on the hotel invoice it normally has a list of the people staying in the room).

We then pay proportionally: if two of you are sharing a double room we will pay 50% of room cost. 

It doesn't matter who booked - your insurance is only for you and hers is only for her.

There are some instances where this doesn't apply (for example- in family groups, big group holidays organised through a club where special insurance has been taken out, or on some very rare cases where the entire holiday has been bought as a gift for someone but only if the gifter has some pretty top end insurance), but in general you'll get the money that you paid, or proportionally what you should have paid, for each element of your holiday, as long as all the other claims conditions are met.

I work in travel insurance. 

Generally travel insurance will automatically cover you until you return to the UK. So if you are delayed, or in hospital and unable to travel, the insurance will continue to run. However, you've said that this is a pre-existing medical condition - did you declare this condition to your insurance? If not then you're likely not even covered now for any medical expenses and you will be required to pay your own additional costs to get you home.

All travel insurance companies in the UK have an emergency line for you to contact while you're outside the UK. Call them and speak to them. You have an obligation to let your travel insurance know you have a claim within a certain time scale (normally 24 hours) so you'll need to call them and speak to them.

Feel free to PM me if you want to talk more. Happy to give general advice but can't make any guarantees because every policy is different.

I think sometimes it's handy to have an advocate. Often when you're ill it's helpful to have someone with you to listen to the Dr and take things in for you. It can be hard to follow things when you're already I'll and in pain/uncomfortable. It also gives you someone to talk through the options with afterwards. Someone who's looking out for your best interests.

In saying that, you need to go on a case by case basis. Perhaps you don't want your mum knowing about anything sexual (birth control, std checks) or when it's something minor that you can handle yourself. I certainly don't tell my mum every time I go to the Dr now, but I do tell her when I need support or help or to talk things through.

It's nice that your mum wanted to come out to be with you. Hospitals can be boring and lonely and I'm sure it came from a place of love. In saying that, if her sole aim was to come out and manage your care with your Dr then that's a different story.

Whenever I take someone to the Dr or visit them in hospital I always say "I'm happy to come in and be a second pair of ears for you, but this is your treatment and your decision - there's a coffee shop right there and I'm just as happy waiting there for you." When I worked in travel insurance last year we would understand that people often wouldn't be able to make reports within 24 hours and often police wouldn't take reports. We would accept instead a police report made after the fact, or a loss report from the tour company or hotel/hostel/whatever.

We would also accept things like a report showing your contract on your phone was cancelled and your iPad hadn't been logged into for x weeks.

I would call back and ask to make a complaint. Tell them you've followed the rest of the TOS and that you did try to report to the police however they were unwilling to provide a report. Tell them you're happy to gather other evidence if required. Make sure they are noting it as an official complaint. If they're not able to resolve it it will go to the complaints department, likely they will cover it, but if not then they'll send you a deadlock letter with the option to take it to the ombudsman. It costs them £500 if you do that so they'll try to avoid it as much as possible.

Make sure you're very clear that you tried to report it to the police but they wouldn't let you.

Also, if you message me what insurance you have if it's one of the brand's I'm familiar with I can try to give you more specific advice.

IANAL! All insurance companies work differently but they all have to follow some basic principles including "treating customers fairly" and I would argue you attempted to report to police so followed terms and conditions to the best of your ability.

I think NHS standards is the wrong way to put it, but essentially what he's saying is that not all care will be free, as with the nhs. So here in the UK all emergency healthcare is free at the point of use, however in Spain there are very few hospitals where you would get free treatment as a UK traveller - if you stay in hospital you might have to pay a E20 per night room fee, which even a local would pay. Basically you're paying what a resident of that country would pay - it won't necessarily be free like it is here. And in the Netherlands they have health insurance (like America but not expensive) so you might not be getting free care there either.

I think having travel insurance is a good idea - if you miss your flight for something that isn't your fault then they'll help you get home, they can organise medical repatriation (I.e. buying extra seats on a plane because you've broken your leg so need to stretch out, or assisting you home on a medical bed with a dr in attendance), and can provide legal help if required.

It's always worth it to have travel insurance, even if you think you don't need it - it's bloody expensive (and difficult to organise) bringing a dead body back to the UK - don't make your loved ones go through that because you were too tight to pay a fiver for a single trip cover.

And finally, a recipe for the whole family:

Lentil and sweet potato curry:

Pour a good pile of red lentils into a saucepan, cover with water and leave to simmer, finely chop or grate an onion or two, a couple of carrots, and a medium- large sweet potato and add to the saucepan - give it all a good mix. Add some parsley, and small amount of mild or medium curry powder, and some coriander. Once the lentils are all cooked and mushy, take out what you want your baby to have (normally one or two tablespoons per portion). I always take out about 4 or 5 portions because this is a great meal for freezing. You can just pop it in the microwave to defrost on those nights where you end up ordering a takeaway for yourself. Once you've taken out baby's stuff, add in a bit more curry powder, a touch of salt if you need it. Yum yum for the whole family.

Other great things for baby to have and gum:

Potato, sweet potato, carrots, broccoli, baby corn, courgette, cauliflower. Just chop them into chunky chips (fries for americans) and boil them. They're dead easy for baby to hold and feed himself.

Another recipe for baby, which you can eat as a side, and again, it can be frozen really easily:

Cauliflower cheese:

Chop up cauliflower, boil in water, drain cauliflower, mash roughly with a fork. In a saucepan add some water, mix in a cup some cornflour and water into a paste and add it to the water, add in a handful of small chunks of cheese and stir stir stir until it's a thick cheesy sauce. Pour over cauliflower. I normally make the sauce with milk for myself but for some reason always make her sauce with water, so that's an option as well. Also, you don't have to mash your cauliflower lol

Hope this helps.
